Lamination of samples was carried out between the silicone coated Mylar substrate on which they were coated, resulting in the samples never coming into contact with the roller of the calendering equipment. The results demonstrated that excellent quality EEA can be prepared via lamination at 90 °C, 25 FPM, and 16,000 pounds separating force, which was achieved with a 6 to 9% reduction of the total EEA stack thickness. As had been previously determined, limiting the amount of passes in the calender is preferred, with high yield and less potential of introducing damage to the EEA laminate surface due to material slipping during processing in the mill. For example, while processing in configuration 1 (layer-by-layer lamination) provided excellent interface contact, it required three passes on the mill as opposed to the other configurations, which limited introduction of processing defects. Surface imperfections may be resolved during binder burn out, under high temperature firing, and this will be investigated in upcoming work. Visual inspection, optical microscopy and SEM imaging of the laminates were used to determine the level of contact at the interface between the layers brought together via lamination. Processing conditions and results are summarized in Table 3 , along with optical images of the fabricated materials. The yellow and red rows in Table 3 were processed with thick ASL layers, while the green rows utilized thin ASL and the reduction in thickness and percentage compression is provided in the table. Conclusions: The optimal manufacturing processing in terms of quality of the EEA stack at this stage of fabrication would be the layer-by-layer deposition via slot-die coating to form the ASL/ASL/AFL assembly followed by lamination of a separately coated GDC electrolyte layer to create the EEA stack, through a single pass of lamination at 90 °C. This allowed for effective EEA fabrication, mild processing temperatures, avoided slot-die coating the thin (~10 μm) electrolyte layer, onto a pre-coated 3-layer substrate, which is prone to surface defects, even at the micron scale, resulting in issues in slot-die coating process. 2.8 Q8 During this quarter, the project has achieved the following:  Prepared 40 ft of individual layers of ASL, AFL and GDC with required thickness for laminating the 10ft EEA.  Started cell performance test at ORNL. Prepared more than 40 ft each of the ASL (~ 300 µm thick), AFL (~ 20 µm thick) and GDC (~ 10 µm) layers with required thickness, waiting for lamination to produce more than 10 ft of laminated ASL/ASL/AFL/GDC layers. At the same time, and for the in-lab performance testing, a TOB bench top 17 calender (up to 120°C) have been used to prepare the ASL/ASL/AFL/GDC EEA.
